The Personal Web Aesthetic

The personal web of the 1990s and early 2000s built a visual culture out of parts: tiled backgrounds, animated dividers, buttons, cliques, adoptables, dolls, and the pages made to hold them. Glitter graphics were one piece of it, and their own story is in . Most of this culture predates glitter or grew up alongside it, but it is the visual and social ground glitter graphics grew out of, and the ground Blingee later drew on more directly.

Net artist Olia Lialina documented this culture in 2005, when its conventions were still recent and much of the material was still online, even though the classic amateur homepage was already receding from the mainstream web. In A Vernacular Web she described a bright, cluttered, homemade web assembled by amateurs out of animated GIFs, tiled backgrounds, MIDI files, construction signs, and whatever else was lying around.[1] The personal web had already normalized treating a page as something built from separate pieces: animated GIFs, tiled backgrounds, decorative text, websets, buttons and badges, dolls and adoptables, graphics collected from other sites, copied HTML snippets, layouts shared as resources, credit and link-back systems, and a collection built up one found or gifted graphic at a time. (The Linkware section below covers how possessive some of that culture actually was.) People got used to encountering graphics as separate, reusable pieces of material, to be found, saved, collected, arranged, credited, traded, and, when the creator allowed it, edited or recombined.

For the broader preservation story and a chronology of the platforms that shaped the personal web, see .

What a Personal Site Was

Personal sites ranged from carefully designed to complete chaos. Plenty of people had real taste and a genuine eye for design, and a personal site was often where that eye got trained, one bad color choice and one too many blinking GIFs at a time. Maximalism was always available, though, and nobody was there to stop you: tiled backgrounds fighting five different fonts, animated glitter piled on more animated glitter, a MIDI file autoplaying whether you asked for it or not. Why wouldn't you post every pretty thing you could find? Personal websites weren't designed by a studio or approved by committee, so a site could be beautifully put together, a complete mess, or both at once depending on which page you clicked into.

Most of the time, you had no idea who was visiting your website. There was something slightly voyeuristic about it: someone could find it through a search engine, a webring, another person's links page, or by clicking around for hours, read everything you had written, and leave without saying a word. Visitor-tracking services such as NedStat, eXTReMe Tracking, and later StatCounter could tell you how many visits you were getting, where people had come from, and sometimes what country or region they were in, but the visitors themselves were still mostly anonymous.

Hit counters made at least one part of that audience visible. A little number at the bottom of the page told you roughly how many times the site had been loaded, and because the counter was usually public, it told everybody else too. A high number could make a site look established or popular in much the same way a follower count does now. Guestbook entries, topsite rankings, and banner clicks offered a few more signs that somebody was actually out there, but none of them told you exactly who was reading.

Search engines increasingly influenced which sites were easiest to find, and Google in particular rewarded pages that other sites linked to. But there was no single feed deciding what everyone saw. People found personal sites through search engines, links pages, directories, webrings, topsites, forums, recommendations, and simply following links from one site to another. There was no platform template forcing every page into the same shape either. One person decided, in Notepad, a WYSIWYG editor, or whatever HTML box their host provided, what their little corner of the internet should look like. Some even wrote a whole "why I made this site" manifesto, sometimes running to genuine essay length, about something they'd built simply because they wanted to. I did it for this site!

Building a Personal Website

GeoCities was the best-known and one of the largest free homepage hosts, but Tripod, Angelfire, Homestead, AOL Hometown, and countless smaller services did the same basic job. Its reputation has also been reinforced by preservation: when Yahoo shut GeoCities down in 2009, outside archivists saved a large share of it, so far more of its old pages remain available to browse than those of many competing hosts. "GeoCities" eventually became shorthand for a whole style of amateur web design: personal sites assembled from whatever graphics, code, and free resources their owner could scrounge up. GeoCities itself leaned hard into the idea of a website as a place of your own. Its users were homesteaders, and early sites lived at numbered addresses inside themed neighborhoods such as Hollywood, Area51, Tokyo, and WestHollywood.[2][3]

Most personal sites were built from basic HTML, a free host's page builder, or a drag-and-drop editor, then decorated with graphics collected from other sites. GeoCities' own drag-and-drop tool was PageBuilder: "Create a cool, full-featured site without any HTML coding. Customize your pages with pictures, sounds, Add-Ons and more. Click 'Launch PageBuilder' to start from scratch, or choose a pre-made template below."[4] Professional web designers worked differently. The common workflow was to design the whole page for an 800 × 600 screen in Photoshop, slice it apart in ImageReady or Fireworks, then rebuild it with HTML tables.[5][6] Those techniques reached hobbyists secondhand, mostly the ones who started taking design seriously, and they were often the same people who moved from free hosts to domains of their own. By the early 2000s, premade table, iframe, and DIV layouts circulated freely, often built around one large image with a tiny scrolling content area dropped into it. Navigation might use an image map or rollover links laid over the artwork. Splash pages asking you to "Enter," microscopic text, custom scrollbars, and layouts built around one photo or illustration became staples of design-heavy personal sites. People kept whole collections of layouts to download, edit, and reuse.[7]

One common trick built a frame out of a 3×3 table. The actual text sat in the center cell while the eight cells around it held pieces of one image, so a block of content could appear to sit inside a glass jar, a pixel-art object, a ripped game sprite, or some other illustrated container. Some designers distributed those table pieces for other people to build with.[8]

Within the more design-heavy personal-domain scene, especially among the girls and young women who often called themselves webmistresses, me/you/site became a recognizable way to organize a whole site.[8] The labels varied, but the split was familiar: me for autobiographical material, you for whatever was on offer to visitors, including adoptables, tutorials, and web graphics, and site for affiliates, cliques, fanlistings, credits, and an archive of previous layouts. Some people used me / you / www, others dressed the same three areas up as the girl / the goods / the www. A homepage might also carry a currently section listing what its owner was eating, watching, listening to, reading, or thinking about that week.

Around 2002, personal-site design changed again. Iframes and image maps became more common, text got even tinier, and navigation became more deliberately organized than the wander-and-discover pages of a few years earlier, which felt cleaner at the time even if some of it has aged terribly. Layouts changed constantly; some people redesigned their entire site every few weeks because they'd learned a new technique or found a style they liked better.

Owners of paid domains often gave other people space on them, and getting that space usually meant applying for it. A domain owner, often called a hostess, gave selected hostees a subdomain, an FTP account, and a small allowance of space and bandwidth, sometimes with MySQL, PHP, CGI, and script installation on top. It generally cost nothing beyond a credit or a link back, but applicants could be judged on their HTML and graphics work, their previous sites, their technical knowledge, and whether the hostess wanted that kind of content on her domain at all. Kawaiiness.com said in 2004 that it was looking for "cute, pixel or visitor based content/cliques/adoption sites," and asked for examples of previous work, FTP and hosting knowledge, and readable English.[8] Having a good .com that other people wanted attached to their name could become a small status symbol, and being hosted on one worked much the same way.

Misa's site, still sitting on a phoophie.com subdomain, is a surviving example of what that could look like. Its red custom scrollbars, custom cursor, and 7pt Georgia still load, and the navigation panels divide neatly into Link In, a row of buttons visitors were told to save to their own servers, and Link Out, described as "lovely sites that I admire, frequent or owe to. Includes affies." Those links lead to other personal subdomains on domains including chewables.org, happy-mix.net, and neonlove.net.

Tiny graphics made specifically for websites included tiled backgrounds, animated dividers, bullets, arrows, clipart, pixel sprites, matching Home / About / Links / Guestbook buttons, hit counters, email graphics, welcome signs, Online / Away / Updated graphics, and flashing "Under Construction" banners. Little "NEW!" icons pointed at whatever had changed. Background MIDI, then WAVs and MP3s, made the page audible too. "Best viewed in Netscape," "Best viewed at 800 × 600," browser badges, HTML-validation buttons, "Made with Notepad" graphics, and dated update logs were familiar fixtures.[9][10][11] A lot of pages also ran small scripts and HTML tricks: marquees, cursor trails, clocks, status-bar messages, disabled right-clicks, rollover images, pop-ups, splash screens, browser-specific entrances. Personal sites rarely felt finished because people kept adding things to them, which probably explains why "Under Construction" survived for so long.

Code moved around almost as freely as the graphics. Funky Chickens HTML Help[12], created in 1999, broke HTML into little effects you could copy straight into your page. Lissa Explains it All was an even earlier pioneer: a colorful, easy-to-follow HTML tutorial site launched in 1997 by 11-year-old Melissa "Lissa" Brown specifically to help kids and beginners build webpages without an automatic page builder. Her notes began on AOL, moved to GeoCities as the site grew, and then moved to their own domain when she was 12. CYP2 / ColorYourProfyle[13] (archived) did something similar for AOL profiles and webpages: color tables, moving and fading text, ALT characters, Wingdings and Webdings, font codes, premade profiles, webpage dolls, and whatever else could be squeezed into AOL's tiny editable boxes. You didn't necessarily sit down to "learn web development." You learned enough HTML to change the background, copied a marquee from somewhere, found a color code somewhere else, broke the page, and eventually figured out why. A lot of that learning was just right-clicking someone's page and hitting "View Source" to see how they'd done something, then lifting the part you needed. That's also the actual reason all those disabled-right-click scripts existed: not a mystery gimmick, just an attempt to stop exactly that. It didn't always work, either as a deterrent or as a lock. At seven years old, I copied code straight off a site that hadn't bothered with one, and still got called out for it in my own guestbook.

Neopets built HTML editing into the site itself. Every Neopet came with its own species-specific petpage, a complete little website whose existing HTML could be edited, rearranged, decorated, or replaced entirely. Neopets allowed users to create editable pet homepages by January 2000, and probably earlier: the earliest surviving official reference is a 14 January 2000 update introducing #OWNER and #OWNERLOOKUP variables for people already designing their pets' homepages, and since Neopets didn't start archiving site updates until that month, the feature's actual launch date is unclear. My suspicion is that Pet Homepages may actually have been a launch-era feature from November or December 1999, when the site itself went up.[14] Neopets also kept a Fun Images[15] library of animated graphics with the HTML already written underneath, ready to copy and paste into petpages, userlookups, shops, and guild pages. Neopets published its own official HTML Guide, released 22 September 2000 as a step-by-step tutorial running from basic tags up through the tables the site's own pages were built on.[16][17] It was marked complete on 5 October 2000, when lessons on banners, tables, and NeoCircles, Neopets' own take on the webring, were added.[18] Introduced that July, NeoCircles were a small HTML snippet that linked petpages, shops, and fan sites sharing a theme.[19] It was a useful way to learn: you did not always have to start with a blank page or understand the code before touching it. You could begin with something that already worked, change it, break it, fix it, and gradually figure out what everything did.

Plenty of Neopets users learned from other players instead. Fan sites taught HTML, CSS, and layouts to other players, and tutorials became part of the fan-site ecosystem: Darkest Faerie Lair taught guild layouts, shops, lookups, and sidebars, and its owner spun the general coding lessons off into Spider's Web Tutorials, a beginner web-design site covering site planning, CSS, HTML, graphics, and layouts.[20][21]

Some pages existed for one specific obsession. A character shrine could be a single dedicated page within a larger personal site, or an entire mini-site of its own, devoted to one character, pairing, series, or other favorite subject. Depending on the corner of the web, the same thing might be called a fan page, fansite, tribute, dedication, or character page instead. Fan pages were widespread by the mid-1990s, and "shrine" circulated in some fandom communities too; it just wasn't a universal personal-web term.

Shrines became especially common in anime and manga fandom. Before anime became much easier to find in the West, the internet was one of the places fans went to find information about series that might never appear on local television or in an ordinary video store. A fan site could have character profiles, episode summaries, image galleries, translations, fan art, fanfiction, and links to fansubs or other sites devoted to the same series. Sometimes you had to already be online to discover any of this in the first place. One anime page led to another, then to a webring or directory, and suddenly there was an entire fandom for something you might never have encountered offline.

"Shrine" has since taken on a broader meaning. Modern Neocities guides may define a "shrine" as any enthusiastically curated page about something the webmaster loves: Pokémon, a book, a tabletop campaign, anything. That meaning is broader than the character- and fandom-specific shrines found on older personal sites, and it has become a standard part of the revival scene's vocabulary. Useful term, but it is a revival-era codification of an old fandom habit, not a label every personal-site owner would have recognized or used at the time.

Graphics, Websets, and Linkware

You did not have to make every graphic or piece of a site yourself. Large libraries existed specifically to supply webmasters with parts. Randy's Icon Bazaar[22] distributed icons. Animation Factory[23] became a major source for the unmistakable rendered animated GIFs and 3D clipart that spread across personal sites. GRSites' Absolute Background Textures Archive[24] (mirror) offered thousands of seamless backgrounds alongside buttons, bullets, arrows, rules, icons, and generated headings.

Graphics creators put together coordinated websets: a matching background, divider bars, bullets, headers, navigation buttons, and usually a small button crediting whoever made the set. Moyra's Web Jewels offered websets and other free graphics alongside hundreds of other sites distributing linkware, custom sets, and freebies.[25][26][27][28]

Sozai (素材, literally "materials") were pixels made to do a job: dividers, bullets, navigation icons, Home and Back and Top and Email graphics, blank buttons for visitors to label themselves, and other small pieces for assembling a page, usually offered in coordinated colors. On me/you/site pages they lived in the you section with everything else laid out for visitors to take. Parts of today's revival scene use the word for almost any tiny sugary pixel graphic, but the older sense was functional.[8]

Linkware was a form of free web graphic distributed on the condition that the person using it linked back to its creator.[26][27] Creators set their own additional terms. They might require a credit button on the same page, forbid alterations, restrict commercial use, ask that a webset remain together, or prohibit redistribution. Permission to use a graphic did not include permission to repost it as part of your own collection. Tutorials and resource lists often directed visitors to the original site rather than re-uploading the files themselves.

The files were supposed to be saved and uploaded to your own server. "DO NOT DIRECT LINK" warnings were common because hotlinking somebody else's GIF made their server deliver it whenever somebody loaded your page, using their bandwidth instead of yours. It was routinely called bandwidth theft. Site owners could block outside requests or replace a hotlinked file with a warning graphic, making the offending site display whatever image the original owner chose to serve. Some creators included blank buttons or matching fonts so a set could be extended without altering the original graphics; others had extremely specific rules about what could be recolored, modified, mixed, or redistributed.

Personal sites often combined backgrounds, fonts, dolls, scripts, brushes, buttons, and other pieces made by different people. Credits and Resources pages listed those sources and linked back to their creators. Attribution was inconsistent, links died, and graphics escaped their original context constantly, but crediting the creator and linking back were established parts of the resource culture.

Layouts were distributed the same way. Creators offered complete layouts for other people to use and customize: change the colors, replace the main image, rewrite the content, keep the bones. The creator's credit and link back generally stayed with the layout, and the creator decided how extensively its code and graphics could be changed. That permission applied to layouts offered as resources, not to any layout somebody happened to see on another person's site. Copying someone's personal design or code without permission, removing somebody else's credit, or presenting their work as your own violated the same rules that applied to graphics. Some creators allowed extensive modification; others were considerably more "DO NOT TAKE MY CODE" about it.

The Social Web Before Social Media

Personal sites had ways for visitors to interact long before social media feeds. Hit counters told you somebody had visited; guestbooks let them leave proof, usually with a name, website address, and sometimes a personalized calling card.[29][30]

By the early 2000s, shoutboxes and tagboards put a tiny public message stream directly on the page, somewhere between a guestbook and live chat. Services such as TagBoard were already turning up on personal sites by 2002, with Cbox following a little later. Site News and Updates pages gave the owner a running place to note whatever had just been added, changed, or redesigned.

Cliques and fanlistings[31] overlapped enough that the distinction could get fuzzy. A fanlisting was, literally, a list of fans of one particular subject, and it did not require a website at all. Cliques were looser. They could be built around an interest, identity, joke, preference, design idea, or some tiny gimmick somebody thought would be fun to pass around, and many expected you to have a site to put the code on. That code did not have to be an image. A text clique might be little more than a word, a heart, and a particular font. The Fanlistings Network opened in May 2000 and became a central directory for fanlistings. A Buffy the Vampire Slayer fanlisting badge still meant, more or less, "I like Buffy." A clique could say "DESIGN WHORE," "I ♥ MY COMPUTER," name your favorite font, assign your website a scent, or invent some other excuse to put one more strange little thing on your page.

Sites at the time drew the lines between these categories differently. Pick Me! divided it in 2004 into cliques, webrings, listings, rotations, exchanges, and fanlistings, and those categories already overlapped while they were in use.[8] In the more design-conscious personal-domain scene, plenty of cliques were far more selective than a copy-and-paste code: applications, rules, member lists, and joining graphics no more than about fifteen pixels high, with "elite" cliques making exclusivity the entire appeal. Some required applicants to own a domain or be hosted on somebody else's, and said outright that Angelfire, Tripod, GeoCities, FreeServers, and the rest of the free hosts would not do.

Some cliques were about the website itself. Scented Angels, which former member Kirryn dates to 1999 and credits to Mandy Clark, who went by Tira, asked members to decide what their current layout would smell like based on its colors and design. A green-and-white layout might be mint, fresh-cut grass, green apple, or, if that was honestly where the design took you, broccoli. Kirryn remembers it at its peak around 2000 and 2001, turning up especially around anime and manga personal sites even though the clique itself had nothing to do with anime. She started Aromatic in 2018 as a reboot rather than a memorial, and it runs as a working clique; her own word for it is reboot, not tribute.[32]

Affiliates, sister or brother sites, and ordinary link exchanges described slightly different relationships between personal sites. An affiliate usually meant some kind of ongoing link exchange, often between sites with similar subjects or audiences. Sister and brother sites could imply a closer relationship between the owners, but the terminology was loose: some people used "sister site," "affiliate," and even "banner exchange" for almost the same arrangement. A simple link exchange could be more impersonal still: you linked me, I linked you, and that was the whole relationship.

In the personal-domain scene, affiliates were often called affies. Two owners arranged it over email, then each displayed the other's little button, commonly around 32×32, on the homepage or in the section about the site itself. It was reciprocal and personal, closer to what would now be called mutuals than to a commercial affiliate program, and some webmasters were as selective about affies as they were about cliques.[8]

Webrings, around since 1994,[33] connected sites on a shared subject into a navigable chain. Previous, Next, Random, and similar links carried visitors from one member to another, so you could start on a Sailor Moon page, keep clicking Next, and eventually work your way through an entire ring of Sailor Moon sites. The ring was a way to actually move around the web, not just a badge of membership.

Some sites kept an entire Joined page for all of this: cliques and fanlistings they belonged to, webrings they'd joined, affiliates, sister sites, campaigns, and whatever other little networks they had accumulated. These pages could run to dozens of buttons and memberships. Read through one and you got a pretty good picture of where that person spent their time online, what they liked, and which other sites they considered part of their neighborhood.

Website awards put one webmaster's approval on another person's page, at least in theory. Some had applications, published criteria, and an actual review before you were allowed to display the graphic. Others were handed out casually, and some were simply offered for anyone to take and put on their own site. Contest-winner badges, challenge awards, and participation graphics looked similar without necessarily meaning the same thing; sometimes you had won something, sometimes you had completed the challenge, and sometimes, with great distinction, you had shown up. Either way, the graphic became a little trophy on your page and often another link back to the person who made or issued it. Some people collected enough of them to need entire awards sections just to display them.

Between fanlistings, cliques, affiliates, sister sites, webrings, and awards, a personal site had many ways to describe a relationship: fan, member, ally, friend, endorsed. None of it had been flattened into one "follow" button.

Personal sites had no built-in likes, shares, or follower counts, but there were plenty of ways to get eyes on one: webrings and blog rings, affiliates and link exchanges, Link Me buttons, credit link-backs from anyone using your graphics, directories, awards, topsites, and banner exchanges. A hit counter told you whether any of it was working. Topsites ranked member sites by visitor votes, so a "Vote for me" button asking people to click through and raise your rank was perfectly normal. Banner exchanges were more mechanical: you displayed other members' banners and, in return, yours appeared across their sites. These were about traffic rather than belonging, closer to the logic of a hit counter but organized and, in the case of topsites, competitive.

Graphics to Collect, Trade, and Display

A lot of these tiny graphics worked as identity markers. An 88×31 button could advertise a website, browser, cause, fandom, or affiliation. Later, stamps, fanlisting buttons, userbars, sig tags, and blinkies could tell you what somebody liked before you'd read a word they'd written. People filled whole pages with them because collecting them was part of the site.

Buttons, Badges, and Blinkies

One of the most characteristic uses of an 88×31 button was pointing back to your own site. A Link Me button meant: save this image to your own server and use it to link to my homepage. Webmasters often offered several designs, and sometimes several sizes, so their buttons would fit neatly alongside whatever a linking site already used. A Link Me button represented the site itself, not an affiliation or a badge of identity. The same 88×31 format was also used for "Best viewed in Netscape" and "Best viewed in Internet Explorer" badges, software and hosting logos, and W3C validation buttons.

The smaller 80×15 antipixel or brilliant button appeared in late 2002 and spread quickly, especially through blogs. Its tiny size made it easy to stack whole rows of them together. They advertised browsers, operating systems, editors, web standards, RSS and Atom feeds, software, directories, hosts, and other sites, but they were just as useful for declaring interests, affiliations, preferences, or jokes. A row of them could end up reading like a miniature profile.

Blinkies came in two main forms. One familiar form was the narrow animated banner, usually around 150×20, with a border or other part of the graphic flashing between frames. Another was built from individual letter blocks, sometimes with tiny icons added, with the letters or blocks lighting up, changing color, bouncing, or moving in sequence. Surviving examples show the block style in use by 2003, particularly around doll sites and later Neopets fansites, and tutorials describe blinkies as being assembled from separate "blocks, icons and letters."[34][35][36] The two forms continued alongside each other rather than one simply replacing the other. The block version is now often called a chain, block, or bead blinkie; Glitter-Graphics still files them under Chain Blinkies.[37][38] On Neocities and other old-web revival sites, "blinkie" more often means the 150×20 banner again, while 88×31 has settled into its own category as a website button.[10][39] The name stayed the same even as the graphic changed.

On me/you/site pages blinkies ran smaller. An 88×15 format was common enough that two of them stacked matched the height of a standard 88×31 button, and thinner versions shrank to around 11 or even 6 pixels high, lettered in pixel fonts such as Bangalore and Redensek.[8] A blinky, as one person put it in 2002, was more or less the web equivalent of a bumper sticker.

Binky Beads, made by Midgee of Namaii in 2001, turned plastic pony-bead bracelets into a tiny web-building kit. Each bead was a 10-pixel square, and the set ran through letters, animals, happy faces, leopard print, and a pile of colors, so you could string together names, words, and bracelet-like strips. People used them on splash pages, as navigation, or dropped straight into a line of text. The original binkybeads.tk later moved to Binky Beads, where the last update is listed as 2004 and the bead vault itself is no longer reachable.[8]

Adoptables and Trading

Adoptables were made to be collected. Artists offered related sets of animals, dolls, fantasy creatures, food, plants, toys, and almost anything else for visitors to adopt, save to their own server, and display on their website with a link back to the creator. Adoption worked as a link exchange as much as a giveaway. In some cases a design could be adopted freely by anybody who wanted it; in others a particular pixel went to one adopter only, handled through email or a web form.[8] The pets themselves, also called cyberpets or virtual pets, might come with names, personalities, certificates, care instructions, or a tiny fictional habitat.

Some mystery eggs and hatchables added an actual surprise. Instead of choosing the finished creature, you adopted an egg and waited to see what it became. Some worked by having the adopter display an image from the artist's server so the artist could later replace the egg file with its hatched form; the URL stayed the same, but the graphic on your page changed. There was no guarantee what you would get. It was a tiny web-graphics gachapon.

Later, clickable adoptables turned the same idea into more of a game. You adopted an egg or pet and put its image and link in a forum signature, profile, or website; other people's views or clicks could help it hatch, grow, get fed, or level up. Dragon Cave[40], launched in 2006, became one of the best-known examples, followed by sites and systems such as Valenth, Squiby, MagiStream, and later PokéFarm. Forum signatures could fill up with creatures waiting for clicks, which helped the pet grow while advertising the adoption site everywhere the owner posted.[41]

People also made graphics specifically for each other. Gifts, freebies, trades, personalized site titles, dolls, buttons, and signatures were part of the social life around personal sites. Someone might keep an entire page of graphics made for them by friends or visitors, with each one linked back to whoever made it.

Toyboxes, Pixel Clubs, and Cliques

All of those little acquisitions needed somewhere to go. A toybox was a page for displaying what you had adopted or been given: pets, food, charms, dolls, toys, gifts, patches, and whatever other tiny pixels had followed you home from somebody else's site, with links back to whoever had made them. Surviving 2003 examples include the adoption toybox on Cathie's Crazie Creations.[8] The name was most at home in the personal-domain and hosted-subdomain pixel scene, though the collecting habit turned up all over. A toybox was a display case, not a club.

Some artists drew toybox pixels specifically for that kind of collection. They were free to take and display under the artist's rules, which did not automatically make them general-purpose web graphics. A pixel offered for somebody's toybox was not necessarily permission to recolor it, drop it into a layout, cut it up into a button, or build it into a collage. As with linkware, "free to use" could come with a surprisingly precise definition of use.

Pixel clubs made the collecting participatory. A club picked a theme, such as teacups, cats, quilt patches, cakes, charms, or lava lamps, and handed out a common template or base for members to work from. You made your own version, put it on your site, and then submitted it, traded it, or collected everybody else's, depending on how that club ran. Everyone started from the same little object; the point was seeing what each person did with it.

Teacups were one version of the format, remembered through the Teahouse MB community and the current Afternoon Tea collection. Kitty Friends, which modern documentation credits to Caz in 2008, used cats instead.

Pixel cliques overlapped with clubs but could be much looser. The shared part might be a size, a subject, a scrap of code, or a gimmick instead of one template everybody edited. Some worked mostly as affiliations; others asked members to make, exchange, or collect a small pixel object.

Pocket Town, created by Lani of Neonlove (archived original), turned a link exchange into a miniature pixel city. Members drew a tiny home or store, linked the building to a website, and arranged the buildings into their own town. Lani described it as "a cute little link exchange in the form of a city community." Buildings had to be between 20×20 and 60×60 pixels, small extras could go in the gaps, files had to be saved to your own server rather than hotlinked, and the main rule was simple: the building itself should always be a link. A modern tribute at Divergent Rays keeps Lani's introduction, rules, and templates and takes new buildings in the same format.[42] I used Neonlove when I was younger, and this is one of the sites I remember from back then.

Other cliques turned the exchange into food and tiny merchandise. Alexandra of miss-behaved.net remembers running Pixel Bakery in 2006 and 2007, where members traded desserts and baked goods they had pixeled themselves.[43] The Yum-Yum Shoppe used a storefront instead: members made their own 15×15 items, put them out for "sale," and collected one another's by displaying them in their own Shoppe with a link back to the owner.[44]

The Quilting Bee (Q*Bee) (archived), founded in 2000 and active through 2014,[45] was one of the more elaborate versions of the idea. Members made patches, 40×40 pixels each, traded them with one another, and "sewed" the patches they received onto pixel quilts displayed on their websites. The club also ran monthly pixel challenges, blog-a-thons, story writing, holiday-card exchanges, and other activities, with patches and pixel mushrooms given out for participating.

The Neocities user lostletters kept a shrine remembering q*bee from the inside, having been a member of both it and Teahouse MB rather than writing about them only after the fact.[46]

Its founder, Gurubii, dated the club to 18 February 2000. Jem, who was already running the club by the October 2007 capture above and was still running it when a 20th-anniversary page went up in 2020, preserved this account of where the idea came from:[45]

It all started on Feb 18 2000 when I was viewing a slander of me on someones site. i was reading in and when i got to the bottom it said "..I pity her, with shame and her quilt." I thought to myself "where does this quilt come into play?" then I was inspired to make a club to connect REAL friends and nice people all together by doing none other than building an internet quilt! this is a club, you join, get your name on the members list, and make new friends! each time you make a friend you exchange your patches and sew them onto your quilt! soon your quilt will be big and beautiful and colorful!

Gurubii, quoted on the club's About page

Membership was conditional and reviewed. An applicant needed a website of their own, a quilt page no more than three clicks from the front page, and a patch they had drawn themselves; the FAQ explicitly refused requests to make the applicant's patch for them.

A panel of members voted submissions up or down, and rejections were common: unoriginal graphics, a personal page with too little on it, text that broke in Firefox, or a missing official membership patch. GeoCities sites were declined as a category, the club explained, not because of the ad banners but because firewalls and ad blockers left them loading as blank pages for many members. The selectivity was deliberate, and the staff said so plainly: admitting everyone would produce thousands of members and a club nobody could manage. Membership ran to roughly 350.

Upkeep fell to the members. Quilts accumulated patches pointing at sites that had moved or disappeared, and pruning them was a recognized chore with a name, washing your quilt. Staff removed inactive members and dead sites from the member list for the same reason. The club changed hands several times across its long run, and most of the personal domains that hosted it along the way have since expired.

Online TCGs turned graphics trading into a game with rules. The community generally credits Senshi Card-Mania!, opened January 22, 2002, as the first fan-run online TCG.[47] Members earned randomized cards through games and site activities, traded duplicates with one another, and kept a trade post on their own website showing what they owned, what they were collecting, and what they had available. Your website was your binder. The hobby eventually produced layouts made specifically for trade posts and scripts for keeping increasingly large collections organized.

Dollz and Pixel Communities

Dolling shared many of the same sites, artists, adoption pages, contests, and trading habits. Its technical lineage reaches back further.

One digital paper-doll lineage predates the web Dollz scene entirely. KiSS (Kisekae Set System) had been in development, according to the KiSS/GS specification for NEC PC-9801VM2 computers since March 1991.[48] A KiSS set packaged a doll and its clothing into its own file format, which could then be opened in a dedicated viewer and dressed by dragging the pieces into place. It began in Japan and spread to other computer platforms during the 1990s, with later versions adding animation, sound, and other interactive features. It belongs to the same larger history of dressing little digital people, but technically it was its own system, with no connection to the graphical chat that web Dollz actually came out of.

The web culture that became known as Dollz grew out of The Palace, the graphical chat system opened to the public in 1995.[49] Palace avatars were assembled from 44×44 graphics called props; a user could wear up to nine at once within a 132×132 area. Early Dollz often used three vertically stacked props for the body, leaving the others for hair, clothing, and accessories. These could be layered onto the body in the Palace prop editor or drawn directly onto the base. Individual Palaces kept collections of saved avatars, often sorted into types like Preps, Sk8rs, Silents, and whatever else that particular community had accumulated. Early names included "lil people" and paper dolls before "Dollz" became the name most widely associated with them on the web.

Once Dollz moved out of The Palace and onto personal websites, they no longer had to work as Palace avatars. GeoCities, Angelfire, and independent domains filled up with finished dolls, downloadable bases, clothing, tutorials, contests, adoptions, requests, and drag-and-drop dollmakers. A dollmaker usually gave you a base surrounded by different hair, clothes, shoes, and accessories to layer onto it, after which the finished doll could be saved and used on your own site. People edited them, traded them, adopted them, entered them into contests, and made new pieces for one another. Crediting the artist who made the base or other parts was an important part of the culture. Dollz Mania (Dollz Mania Backup) and The Doll Palace (archived) became two of the larger sites in a much wider network of personal Dollz sites.[50][51]

By the early 2000s, dolling had also become a digital-art hobby of its own. Some artists drew whole bases, clothing, hair, and poses themselves, either from scratch or on top of another artist's credited base. In parts of the community, dolls or pixel dolls became preferable to "Dollz" for this kind of work, partly to distinguish hand-drawn dolls from those assembled in a dollmaker. The terminology was never very tidy. "Dollz," "dolls," "pixel dolls," and "cartoon dollz" all turn up, and "dolls" alone is a terrible search term if what you actually want is a tiny illustrated person from somebody's 2003 homepage. More specific names often tell you more anyway: Preps, Sk8rs, Silents, Minis, Wonderkins, Divas, and plenty of others referred to recognizable body styles, poses, or base families.

What English-language doll sites later called Korean Dollz came from a different kind of system. Korean community and gaming sites were building commercial avatar systems around the turn of the 2000s. SayClub began offering avatars in 2000 and started selling clothing and accessories for them that November; Freechal, Cyworld, and other services developed their own avatar economies around the same period. These were not open bases for hobbyists to draw on. The bodies, hairstyles, clothing, and accessories were professionally made for the service, and users built an avatar from the pieces available to them, often buying individual items as virtual goods. Cyworld's MiniMe lived inside the user's minihompy and decorated miniroom, so the avatar became part of both the user's appearance and the little space they built around it.

Candybar[52] was one of the Korean avatar systems that became especially visible to Western doll sites. Developed by Neople, it opened in beta on 21 December 2001 as an avatar and gaming portal, with games including Love Love Studio and Kung Kung Tta. Around 2004, its artwork began circulating much more widely in English-language dolling through eLouai's unofficial Candybar Doll Maker.[53] eLouai took the existing Candybar assets and turned them into a browser-based dress-up maker, letting users combine the bodies, faces, hair, clothes, shoes, accessories, pets, backgrounds, and other pieces that Candybar's artists had already drawn.

Candybar built its avatars as a stack of transparent GIF layers rather than as a single pre-rendered image. The avatar area was fixed at 150 × 290 pixels and contained 32 image slots, numbered from Layer 0 through Layer 31. Unused slots loaded a transparent placeholder, while clothing, hair, body parts, accessories, and other elements were swapped into specific positions in the stack. The layer structure also allowed a single item to be split across multiple depths, so one part could appear behind the avatar while another appeared in front. Hidden form fields stored which item occupied each layer, meaning the site maintained the avatar as structured data as well as a visual stack of images. Because every asset appears to have shared the same coordinate space, Candybar could assemble and update the character dynamically in the browser without generating a new flattened image after every change.

The basic idea was somewhat similar to The Palace, where multiple props could be layered over a base doll, although Candybar used a much more rigid slot and coordinate system for assembling the avatar.

Dollers regularly drew new clothing, hair, bases, and accessories for one another, but Candybar users mostly worked with the existing Candybar library. The artwork was much denser and more detailed than most of the small hand-drawn Dollz circulating on personal sites, with carefully shaded clothes, tiny accessories, glossy highlights, and comparatively large heads. Reproducing that style well was difficult, and making new Candybar-compatible pieces was never the main activity. The attraction was the enormous collection of professionally drawn parts that were already there to combine. People sometimes edited a finished avatar afterward, but they generally were not building a new Candybar wardrobe themselves.

Western sites still absorbed the finished avatars into Dollz culture, collecting them beside Preps, Silents, pixel dolls, and other styles. "Korean Dollz" seems to have been mainly an English-language collector term; the Korean services themselves generally called them avatars and the individual clothes and accessories avatar items. Candybar was only one source. Similar graphics came from services including Cyworld, SayClub, Netmarble, Hangame, Daum, Buddy Buddy, and Freechal. Much of that material is harder to reconstruct now because the original avatar systems were tied to user accounts and pages the Wayback Machine could not fully reach.

Forums, Messaging, and Profiles

Forums, AIM, LiveJournal, and later MySpace ran alongside personal domains for years. Website buttons became profile badges and stamps. Guestbooks and comments coexisted. Doll and pixel-art communities appeared in avatars and icons as easily as on a homepage. Graphics sites added Photoshop brushes, textures, and templates beside the older GIFs and websets, serving whichever platform you happened to be decorating that week.

Forums offered two main spots to customize: an avatar beside your username and a signature under your posts. They could match as a set or have nothing to do with each other. Graphics boards often bundled requests for both, handled by the same pool of designers.

Avatar and icon sizes depended on the platform, and people kept accounts and icons on several platforms at once. Forum avatars followed whatever limits the board imposed. AIM buddy icons ran 48×48 or 50×50, MSN Messenger display pictures were 96×96, and LiveJournal userpics were 100×100. Dedicated sites supplied all of it, collecting AIM icons, MSN pictures, Yahoo smileys, and away messages by the thousands.

Signatures were the customizable block automatically attached beneath forum posts. They could be one line of text or a quote, but people often treated the space like a miniature profile: custom graphics, usernames, favorite characters, animations, links, whatever the board's limits allowed. Making signatures became its own branch of web graphics. You could make one yourself, ask a friend, or post in a request thread where a designer took your username, character or image, colors, text, and general direction, then posted the finished version back, sometimes with revisions or several options.

The graphic inside a forum signature was often called a sig tag. It usually centered on a character or other artwork, sometimes with a name or username worked into the design. People made them in programs such as Paint Shop Pro and Photoshop using swirl, grunge, sparkle, and vector brushes, along with pixel art, glitter, decorative type, and Paint Shop Pro tubes. You generally used one until you made or requested a new one to replace it.

Salvaged, maintained by Belle, archives brushes from older graphics programs, including the kinds of assets used to make graphics like these.

By the mid-2000s, userbars were a forum-signature staple: long, thin 350×19 banners, usually with a tiny image on one side and text on the other, announcing whatever the bar was about. Because they were only 19 pixels tall, you could stack several of them inside a forum's signature-height limit. They were also much easier to collect and swap around than a full custom signature graphic.

Unlike most of these formats, stamps have a documented origin. DeviantArt's then-creative director Ryan Ford created the format for the 2005 DeviantArt Summit, originally planned for an airplane hangar; the little air-mail or postage-style badge made sense for the event. The two earliest recovered examples were posted on April 22, 2005.[54] The standard became a 99×56 graphic framed by that recognizable perforated postage-stamp border, either static or animated.

Users almost immediately turned stamps into tiny visual bumper stickers for their identities and opinions. They covered fandoms, ships, software, music, games, political and social views, characters, aesthetics, jokes, and every variety of "I support…" or "Proud ___" declaration. Some had edgy Happy Bunny or Spencer's-tee energy; others were practical DeviantArt etiquette, telling visitors to view the full artwork, not steal it, leave feedback, stop repeatedly viewing a page without watching the account, or check whether requests and commissions were open.

The stamp was usually uploaded as a DeviantArt deviation of its own. Other users didn't have to save and re-upload the GIF to display it. They could embed the original deviation with thumbnail syntax such as :thumb427548925:, so the stamp on their profile still pointed back to the creator's submission.

Iconator[55] collected huge libraries of AIM buddy icons, avatars, wallpapers, and away messages. Glitter-Graphics.com[56] and Dazzle Junction[57][58] supplied glitter text, backgrounds, layouts, and copy-and-paste code for MySpace and other profile sites. FlamingText[59] generated customized headings and animated text from whatever you typed into the box. The surface changed; the habit didn't. Forums, LiveJournal, Xanga, Piczo, Gaia, Neopets, MySpace, and AIM each gave people a slightly different place to put an avatar, a signature, a background, a profile layout, a comment, a badge, personalized text, or an identity graphic: the same handful of behaviors turning up again on a new surface every time users moved somewhere new.

You could take a background from one graphics site, a premade iframe layout from another teenager, learn how to change its scrollbar from Funky Chickens, grab an ALT character from CYP2, add an official Neopets GIF linked with your referral, put a Candybar doll beside the guestbook, and finish with a row of buttons linking back to everybody whose work you'd used. Of course it looked eclectic. Half the page came from different people.

A lot of the socializing happened through the graphics themselves. A button sent you to somebody else's site; an award showed that another webmaster had approved of yours; a sig tag or blinkie said something about you without a paragraph of explanation. Even a tiled background could carry one person's work into hundreds of other people's websites.

Some formats were defined by their exact dimensions:

Format Common / canonical size Why this size?
Website button ("Link Me") 88×31 Popularized by early web badges, including Netscape's promotional buttons, and later recognized by the IAB as the "Micro Bar." The exact dimensions were a convention rather than a browser limitation.
Antipixel button 80×15 Established by Jeremy Hedley's Antipixel buttons in the early 2000s. The deliberately tiny format worked well for weblog sidebars and spread as a reusable template rather than because of a technical restriction.
Fanlisting code 50×50, 75×50, 100×35, 100×50 (sometimes 88×31 or 200×40) There was no single required size. Fanlistings offered several standardized code sizes so members could choose one that fit their own site's layout, and those dimensions became conventions across the community.
DeviantArt stamp 99×56 Originated with DeviantArt's 2005 Summit promotion as a tiny digital stamp or bumper sticker. The original 99×56 template was copied for user-made stamps until the dimensions became part of the format; it was not a DeviantArt image-size limit.
Userbar 350×19 Designed for forum signatures: wide enough for a label and small graphic, but short enough that several could be stacked without taking over a post. The exact 350×19 dimensions became a community template standard rather than a universal forum restriction.
Banner blinkie 150×20 The classic blinkie template was long enough for a short line of animated text while remaining tiny enough to stack with other graphics. The dimensions were a community convention, not a Neocities restriction.
Quilting Bee patch 40×40 A club standard rather than a technical one. A fixed square meant every member's patch sat the same size in everybody else's quilt, so a page of traded patches tiled into an even grid however many people you had swapped with.
Web banner (banner exchange) 468×60 Standardized as the web advertising "full banner," allowing the same ad to circulate through banner exchanges and unrelated websites without being resized. It was later formalized as an IAB standard ad size.
AIM buddy icon 48×48 or 50×50 A client-imposed small icon size that suited a compact chat interface, in line with contemporary desktop interface icons of the time. AOL does not appear to have documented why it chose exactly 48–50 pixels.
MSN display picture 96×96 Messenger displayed and resized profile pictures to 96×96 as part of its interface design. Microsoft does not appear to have documented why it chose exactly 96 pixels.
LiveJournal userpic 100×100 A platform maximum suited to LiveJournal's text-heavy layout: large enough to work as an expressive image, but small enough to appear repeatedly beside posts and comments. The site's interface became heavily structured around the 100×100 limit, although the original reason for choosing exactly 100 pixels does not appear to be documented.
The Palace prop / maximum avatar area 44×44 / 132×132 The Palace was built around a fixed 44×44 sprite tile: the default roundhead and each wearable prop occupied one tile. An avatar could combine up to nine props across a 3×3 area, producing the 132×132 maximum. The reason 44 pixels specifically was chosen does not appear to be documented.

The End of the Personal Web

Between personal websites and standardized social media came a middle stage of customizable, centralized profiles, and MySpace is the important transitional case. Writing in 2007, Lialina described people moving out of standalone homepages into "the language of MySpace" (accounts, profiles, journals, channels), and pointed out how much those new pages still resembled their Web 1.0 predecessors: a background, blocks of graphics, text, and video laid over it, held together by the same modular, HTML-based aesthetic.[60] MySpace centralized identity and social interaction inside one company's service, but it still let users control how their own page looked, an extension of the homepage habit more than a break from it. Facebook[61] allowed almost none of that personalization. The broader shift called Web 2.0[62] emphasized user-generated content inside centralized services, and as that model developed, many major platforms also took more control over how user-created material looked. As users migrated further into standardized social networks, the personal homepage began to look antiquated.

Lycos kept the remaining Tripod and Angelfire sites online long after the free-hosting era ended, then took them down on 24 April 2026, ending nearly three decades of web hosting. The shutdown notice appeared on the Lycos homepage in March, vanished while staying in the page source, and came back in April.[63] The full chronology is on the timeline.

Glitter graphics outlived the homepage. How they moved on to profiles, to Blingee, and to messaging apps is in .

  • The Garden of Madeline. "Pixel Clubs". Modern explanation and examples of the themed-template pixel-club format.
  • Little Vampire. "Toybox". Current toybox spelling out which collected pixels may and may not be reused elsewhere.
Collections & Community Documentation
  • Leonard Wojcik. "88 × 31".
  • Reddit / r/neocities. "Question About Blinkies". 2026 discussion of bead/block blinkies and modern banner blinkies.
  • NekoDirectory. "Web Clique Directory". Directory of historical and current web cliques, including pixel and text cliques and the Japanese term 同盟 (dōmei).
  • Reef. "Mini-Cliques". Current collection of pixel and text cliques with copyable joining codes.
  • Kirryn. "Aromatic". 2018 reboot of the Scented Angels design clique by a former member, with a retrospective history of the original.
  • Ainna. "SCENTED". 2019 homage to Scented Angels whose creator explicitly declines to call it a revival.
  • Divergent Rays. "Pocket Town". Modern tribute preserving Lani's Pocket Town rules and templates and accepting new pixel buildings.
  • Alexandra. "The Museum of Alexandra: History". Personal history documenting Q*Bee membership, the 2006–2007 Pixel Bakery clique, and text cliques.
  • Alexandra. "Afternoon Tea". Current teacup pixel-club collection documenting its connection to the older Teahouse MB clique.
  • Fairytrash. "The Yum-Yum Shoppe". Preservation and recreation of a 2000s pixel clique built on making, "selling," collecting, and linking 15×15 pixel items.
  • Namaii / Midgee. "Binky Beads". Pixel bead system created in 2001 and migrated from the original binkybeads.tk domain; the current page lists its last update as 2004.
  • Hexed Pixels. "Hexed Pixels". Site of a former Q*Bee member.
